background: Edge-weighted online bipartite matching with free disposal is a clean abstraction of display advertising and related allocation systems. Offline vertices are reusable only in the sense that they may keep the best offer seen so far: if a later online vertex gives a better edge weight, the old tentative match can be discarded without penalty. This free-disposal rule makes the problem easier than irrevocable edge-weighted matching, but still far harder than unweighted or vertex-weighted matching. The trivial greedy algorithm is $1/2$-competitive, and for years no algorithm beat that barrier. The breakthrough came from online correlated selection, a randomized subroutine that deliberately correlates choices across time. The exact competitive ratio remains wide open: the best algorithms are only slightly above $1/2$, while the natural upper bound remains the classical $1-1/e$ scale.
short_statement: Online arrivals reveal arbitrary edge weights, while each offline vertex retains only its best assigned edge. The best checked guarantee is now $0.556195$.
full_statement: Let $G=(L,R,E)$ be a bipartite graph. The offline side $L$ is known in advance, while vertices of $R$ arrive one at a time in an adversarial order. When online vertex $v\in R$ arrives, all incident edge weights $w_{uv}\ge 0$ for $u\in L$ are revealed. The algorithm may either discard $v$ or assign it immediately to one offline vertex $u$. Assignments are irrevocable from the perspective of the arriving vertex, but offline vertices have free disposal: an offline vertex may receive many online vertices over time and contributes only $\max\{w_{uv}:v\text{ assigned to }u\}$ to the final objective, with value $0$ if no vertex is assigned to it. Equivalently, an advertiser may keep the best impression ever assigned and ignore lower-value previous assignments. The benchmark is the maximum-weight offline matching in $G$, which can assign at most one online vertex to each offline vertex after seeing the entire graph and arrival sequence. For randomized algorithms, the expectation is over the algorithm's internal randomness against an oblivious adversary that fixes the entire graph, edge weights, and arrival order independently of the random coins. Determine the supremum competitive ratio $\alpha$ such that an online algorithm always obtains expected retained weight at least $\alpha\cdot\mathrm{OPT}$.
known_results:
Greedy is $1/2$-competitive. Matthew Fahrbach, Zhiyi Huang, Runzhou Tao, and Morteza Zadimoghaddam first surpassed this with $0.5086$; Guy Blanc and Moses Charikar raised the guarantee to $0.5368$ using multiway online correlated selection.

Alireza Farhadi and Mohammad Hajiaghayi, 'Online Edge-Weighted Matching Beyond 0.55' (arXiv:2611.06896v1, November 2026), Theorem 1, give $0.556195$ against an oblivious adversary for arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. Rational inputs admit an expected-polynomial-time implementation. Their tightness analysis concerns their algorithm, not every online policy; their formal certificates were not replayed in this audit.

Remaining open problem. Determine the optimal ratio in $[0.556195,1-1/e]$. The upper endpoint follows already from unweighted online matching. Guarantees for product-structured weights or limitations of a particular correlation scheme do not close this general gap.
open_problem: Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary: close the gap between $0.556195$ and $1-1/e$.

counterexample_rationale: Hard instances and limitations of OCS formulations can be encoded as finite weighted graphs and adversarial arrival distributions. Search may find stronger upper-bound gadgets or reveal why known OCS frameworks stall.
alphaevolve_rationale: This is one of the more code-search-friendly online matching problems: factor-revealing programs, OCS parameter searches, and finite weighted hard instances are all computationally accessible.

literature.synthesis: Free disposal makes each offline vertex's contribution a retained maximum. Correlations across repeated choices and threshold-based primal-dual accounting have successively improved guarantees. The new bound belongs in that progression, while framework-specific tightness must remain separate from a universal impossibility result.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Search for richer online correlated selection primitives, stronger factor-revealing relaxations, or adversarial weighted gadgets that cap all algorithms. A useful intermediate target is to prove tightness for a restricted class of OCS-based algorithms.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: For an algorithmic improvement, verify the model includes free disposal and arbitrary edge weights, not only vertex weights, unweighted edges, stochastic arrivals, or bounded capacities. The proof must compare expected retained maximum edge weight at each offline vertex against the offline maximum-weight matching. If the algorithm uses OCS, the correlation guarantee must hold online for every adaptive sequence of candidate sets generated by the matching algorithm, and the primal-dual or factor-revealing analysis must cover all weight levels, including ties and zero weights. For an upper bound, the hard instance must be a distribution over finite weighted bipartite graphs and arrival orders; by Yao's principle it must bound every deterministic online policy, not merely Greedy, Ranking, or a named OCS family. A limitation of a restricted framework should be labeled as such and should not be presented as a global impossibility theorem.
